K(4, 1) is the complete graph on four singletons; K(4, 2) is three separate edges, each pair joined to its complement; K(5, 2) is the Petersen graph on the ten pairs from 0 to 4." width="100%"} Creates one node for every `k`-element subset of `{0, 1, ..., n-1}` and joins two nodes when their subsets are disjoint. The graph has `C(n, k)` nodes ("n choose k"), and each node has degree `C(n - k, k)`. `K(n, 1)` is the complete graph on `n` nodes, `K(5, 2)` is the Petersen graph, and when `n < 2k` no two subsets are disjoint, so there are no edges. Lovász proved that the chromatic number of `K(n, k)` is `n - 2k + 2`, a celebrated result of topological combinatorics. Each node is labelled with the elements of its subset, comma-separated and in increasing order (e.g. `"0,2"`), and nodes are created in lexicographic order of their subsets. In a directed graph each edge points from the earlier subset to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. The Johnson graph (see `add_johnson_graph()`) uses the same nodes but joins subsets that overlap in all but one element. Kneser graphs are useful for: - examples in graph coloring and combinatorics with known chromatic numbers - modeling conflict-free pairings: nodes are fixed-size teams drawn from a pool, and an edge means two teams share no member and can play at the same time - test cases for highly symmetric, regular graphs ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of the base set `{0, 1, ..., n-1}`. Must be at least `1`. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of each subset. Must satisfy `1 <= k <= n`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each node is labelled with its subset as described above. Because these labels don't depend on the existing nodes, adding a second labelled Kneser or Johnson graph with overlapping subsets raises `ValueError` (labels are unique); pass `label=False` for the second one. If `False`, nodes are created without labels. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `1` or `k=` is not between `1` and `n=`. ::: ## Complexity {.doc-complexity} Every pair of subsets is compared, so the time grows as `C(n, k)^2`. `C(n, k)` grows very quickly (e.g. `C(20, 10)` is 184,756), so keep `n=` modest when `k=` is near `n / 2`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `K(5, 2)` has `C(5, 2) = 10` nodes, each joined to the `C(3, 2) = 3` pairs disjoint from it, which makes it the Petersen graph: ::: {#b9b6fe67 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_kneser_graph(n=5, k=2) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges(), graph.is_isomorphic( ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 15, True) ``` ::: ::: The neighbors of `"0,1"` are exactly the pairs drawn from `{2, 3, 4}`: ::: {#506c7fdc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} sorted(graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.get_neighbors("0,1")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['2,3', '2,4', '3,4'] ``` ::: :::
